note: John never calls Jesus' miracles “acts of power” (*dynameis*), the Synoptic word. He calls them **signs**: {jn 2:11 ἀρχὴν τῶν σημείων} (“the beginning of the signs”). They point beyond themselves, here to abundance (about 120–180 gallons of wine). Jesus' reply to his mother, {jn 2:4 οὔπω ἥκει ἡ ὥρα μου} (“my hour has not yet come”), introduces John's countdown to the “hour” of the cross.

The conversation turns on a Greek double meaning. {jn 3:3 γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν} can mean “born **again**” or “born **from above**”; Nicodemus hears the first, Jesus means the second. John often builds dialogues on such misunderstandings. In this Gospel the narrator's voice blends into Jesus' speech, and it is unclear where Jesus stops speaking and the narrator begins, possibly before the famous {jn 3:16 Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον}.

In the other Gospels John the Baptist is a fiery prophet of judgment. In John he is purely a **witness** who points away from himself: {jn 3:30 ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι} (“he must increase, I must decrease”). This Gospel also has Jesus' and John's ministries running at the same time, with both baptizing, where Mark has Jesus begin only after John's arrest (Mark 1:14).

The longest conversation Jesus has with anyone in the Gospels is with a Samaritan woman, someone a Jewish teacher would normally avoid on two counts: {jn 4:9 οὐ γὰρ συγχρῶνται Ἰουδαῖοι Σαμαρίταις} (“Jews do not associate with Samaritans”). {jn 4:10 ὕδωρ ζῶν} (*hydōr zōn*) means both “running water” and “living water”, another Johannine double meaning. The scene ends with Jesus' first plain self-identification, {jn 4:26 Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ λαλῶν σοι} (“I am he, the one speaking to you”).

A Sabbath healing in Jerusalem sparks the conflict that drives the rest of John's Gospel. Jesus' defense, {jn 5:17 Ὁ πατήρ μου ἕως ἄρτι ἐργάζεται κἀγὼ ἐργάζομαι} (“my Father is working until now, and I am working”), is heard as a claim to be {jn 5:18 ἴσον ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν τῷ θεῷ} (“making himself equal to God”). Verse 4, about an angel stirring the water, is absent from the oldest manuscripts; see the Variants page.

A long discourse on the Son's authority to give life and to judge. John's characteristic idea is **“realized eschatology”**: eternal life is not only future but present. Whoever believes {jn 5:24 ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον} (“*has* eternal life”, present tense) and {jn 5:24 μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν} (“has already crossed over from death to life”, a perfect tense).

After the feeding miracle, which all four Gospels tell, John alone adds this long discourse. Its first of John's seven “I am” sayings with a predicate, {jn 6:35 Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς} (“I am the bread of life”), turns into strongly physical language: {jn 6:53 φάγητε τὴν σάρκα} (“eat the flesh”). John has no Last Supper institution of the bread and wine, and many readers see eucharistic language placed here instead.

A frank remark that the other Gospels lack: {jn 7:5 οὐδὲ γὰρ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ ἐπίστευον εἰς αὐτόν} (“not even his brothers believed in him”). Mark 3:21 has his family trying to restrain him. Jesus first says he is not going up to the festival, then goes in secret, an apparent inconsistency some early scribes eased by changing “not” (*ouk*) to “not yet” (*oupō*) in verse 8. Many commentators read “not going up” as “not now” or “not publicly, with you”, which is exactly how he then goes.

Jesus teaches in the temple at the autumn Feast of Tabernacles, whose rituals included water-pouring and great lamps. His sayings about living water (7:37–38) and, in the next chapter, light play on these ceremonies. The debate is a three-way argument over his origins, among the crowds, the authorities and their own guards, who come back empty-handed: {jn 7:46 Οὐδέποτε ἐλάλησεν οὕτως ἄνθρωπος} (“no one ever spoke like this man”).

This famous story is absent from the earliest manuscripts of John, and modern editions print it in double brackets. Its vocabulary also reads more like Luke than John. Some manuscripts place it after Luke 21:38. The Gospels never say what Jesus wrote: {jn 8:6 τῷ δακτύλῳ ἔγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν} (“with his finger he wrote on the ground”). His one line, {jn 8:7 Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτον ἐπ᾿ αὐτὴν τὸν λίθον βαλέτω}, became proverbial.

The most heated confrontation in the Gospels ends with a sentence that breaks grammar on purpose: {jn 8:58 πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι ἐγὼ εἰμί} (“before Abraham came to be, I am”). Abraham's coming into being is an aorist; Jesus' existence is a timeless present, echoing God's self-name in Exodus 3:14 (Septuagint *egō eimi*). The listeners pick up stones, the response to blasphemy.

A story about who truly sees. The blind man's parents are afraid of being made {jn 9:22 ἀποσυνάγωγος} (*aposynagōgos*, “expelled from the synagogue”), a word found nowhere before John and nowhere else in the New Testament outside John. Many scholars read it as reflecting the experience of John's own community late in the first century, projected back into Jesus' lifetime. Others point out that synagogues already had disciplinary exclusion in Jesus' day, so the threat need not be anachronistic.

{jn 10:11 Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός} uses *kalos*, which means “good” in the sense of “fine, noble, model”, rather than the moral word *agathos*. The image draws on Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's bad shepherds and promises to shepherd the flock himself. The defining act of this shepherd is the one no hired hand would do: {jn 10:11 τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ τίθησιν} (“lays down his life”).

Set at Hanukkah, the festival of the temple's rededication. The climactic {jn 10:30 ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν} (“I and the Father are one”) uses the **neuter** *hen*, “one thing”, not the masculine *heis*, “one person”. Later Christian debates about the Trinity leaned heavily on that grammatical detail.

The seventh and greatest sign, and in John the event that triggers Jesus' death, a role the Synoptics give to the temple incident. It contains both the shortest verse in most English Bibles, {jn 11:35 ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς} (“Jesus wept”), and one of the boldest claims, {jn 11:25 Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή} (“I am the resurrection and the life”). Caiaphas then unknowingly prophesies that one man should die {jn 11:50 ὑπὲρ τοῦ λαοῦ} (“for the people”).

A short, dark note found only in John: the chief priests plan {jn 12:10 ἵνα καὶ τὸν Λάζαρον ἀποκτείνωσιν} (“to kill Lazarus too”), since he is living evidence drawing people to Jesus. The little word *kai* (“also”) carries the irony: a man raised from death is now marked for death again.

When Greeks ask to see Jesus, he answers that {jn 12:23 Ἐλήλυθεν ἡ ὥρα} (“the hour has come”), the hour that had “not yet come” at Cana. The single seed that must die to bear fruit replaces the Synoptic Gethsemane agony. John also turns “lifted up”, {jn 12:32 ἐὰν ὑψωθῶ}, into a double meaning: lifted up on the cross, and exalted in glory.

The narrator closes Jesus' public ministry by quoting Isaiah 6 on hardened hearts, a passage the Synoptics use for the parables. Then comes a startling claim: {jn 12:41 ταῦτα εἶπεν Ἠσαΐας ὅτι εἶδεν τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ} (“Isaiah said this because he saw *his* glory”). In context “his” refers to Jesus, so the vision of the Lord on his throne in Isaiah 6 is read as a vision of Christ.

Where the Synoptics have the bread and cup at the Last Supper, John has Jesus wash the disciples' feet, a slave's task. The lesson is explicit: {jn 13:14 καὶ ὑμεῖς ὀφείλετε ἀλλήλων νίπτειν τοὺς πόδας} (“you also ought to wash one another's feet”). John also dates this meal **before** Passover, so that Jesus dies as the Passover lambs are being slaughtered, a well-known difference from the Synoptic chronology. Harmonizers suggest that different groups followed different calendars, or that John's “Passover” refers to the whole festival week.

Jesus' farewell discourse, a genre with Old Testament models such as Jacob's and Moses' final speeches. It introduces the {jn 14:16 ἄλλον παράκλητον} (*paraklētos*), a legal term for someone called to your side: advocate, helper or counselor. “Another” implies that Jesus has been the first. The chapter also holds the exclusive claim {jn 14:6 Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωή}.

The vine image, {jn 15:1 Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος ἡ ἀληθινή} (“I am the **true** vine”), takes over a symbol the prophets used for Israel, the vineyard God planted. The key verb is *menō*, “remain, abide”, which appears ten times in seven verses (15:4–10). John uses it far more often than any other Gospel; it is one of his statistical fingerprints.

Some readers see a seam here. At the end of chapter 14 Jesus says “Rise, let us go from here” (14:31), yet the discourse continues for three more chapters. Many scholars think the farewell speeches were expanded in stages. The traditional reading is simpler: Jesus kept teaching as they left the room and walked toward the Kidron valley (18:1). This section ends on a note of victory before the arrest: {jn 16:33 ἐγὼ νενίκηκα τὸν κόσμον} (“I have conquered the world”), in the perfect tense, as already accomplished.

Jesus' longest prayer anywhere in the Gospels. Instead of Gethsemane's “let this cup pass”, John's Jesus prays calmly for his followers' unity: {jn 17:21 ἵνα πάντες ἓν ὦσιν} (“that they may all be one”). Eternal life is defined here as **knowing**: {jn 17:3 ἵνα γινώσκωσι σὲ τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεὸν} (“that they may know you, the only true God”).

“Doubting Thomas” delivers the highest confession of Jesus in any Gospel: {jn 20:28 Ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου} (“my Lord and my God”). That brings John full circle from {jn 1:1 θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος} in the first verse. Jesus' reply looks beyond the story to later readers, who believe without seeing: {jn 20:29 μακάριοι οἱ μὴ ἰδόντες καὶ πιστεύσαντες}.

John states his purpose outright: {jn 20:31 ταῦτα δὲ γέγραπται ἵνα πιστεύητε} (“these things are written so that you may believe”). The manuscripts are divided between the present subjunctive *pisteuēte* (“keep on believing”) and the aorist *pisteusēte* (“come to believe”), so it is debated whether John wrote for believers or for outsiders. This sounds like a book's ending, and most scholars think chapter 21 was added later. No manuscript lacks it, and traditional readers take it as the author's own epilogue.

Three questions answer Peter's three denials. Jesus twice asks {jn 21:15 ἀγαπᾷς με} using *agapaō*, and Peter answers with *phileō*; the third time Jesus switches to Peter's verb, {jn 21:17 φιλεῖς με}. Preachers often make much of the change, but John uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere, and he varies other words here too (lambs/sheep, feed/tend), so many scholars see stylistic variety rather than a coded distinction.

The closing verses shift voice: “**we** know that his testimony is true”, then “**I** suppose” ({jn 21:25 οἶμαι}). Others are vouching for the Beloved Disciple, which suggests a community or editor finished the book. The appendix corrects a rumor that this disciple would not die ({jn 21:23 ὁ μαθητὴς ἐκεῖνος οὐκ ἀποθνῄσκει}), perhaps because he had recently died. From Irenaeus onward, tradition has identified this disciple as John son of Zebedee, writing in old age at Ephesus.
